newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to play NATO expansion card in Washington.
newsitem.headline: Russia to play NATO expansion card in Washington.

text.p: Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Sunday that he would remind the gatekeepers of the world's elite economic clubs this week of Moscow's firm opposition to NATO expansion plans.

In the most overt linkage yet by a Russian official between NATO expansion and economic concessions Moscow is hoping to win from the West, Chubais said the NATO plan was a "pointless and dangerous attempt to isolate Russia from the civilised world".

"To stop that danger materialising, we are obliged to work out with the respective leaders, including those of the United States, mechanisms to compensate for that danger and loss Russia will suffer on the world political arena from NATO expansion," said Chubais, quoted by Interfax news agency.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation is expected, at a summit in Madrid in July, to invite Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to begin entry talks.

Speaking to reporters on his way to the spring meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Washington, Chubais said he would discuss Russia's entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and Paris Club of government creditors.

U.S. President Bill Clinton pledged last month to work to get Russia into the Paris Club this year and the WTO in 1998. But Russia has to meet a string of conditions for entry, which do not depend on Washington alone.

Chubais, who hopes membership of the Paris Club will help Russia recover funds lent by the Soviet Union under communism to Third World states, said he would get tough with some of the debtors when he meets their finance ministers in Washington.
Russia could get back around $300-500 million a year from around 27 debtor nations, Interfax quoted Chubais as saying on the plane on his way to the United States.

Moscow also wants the United States to exclude it from its Jackson-Vanik amendment, which blocks Most Favoured Nation trading status for any country that does not have open emigration policies, a category into which Russia has historically fallen.
"It is discriminatory in relation to Russia and remains such on the American market even if Russia enters the WTO," Interfax quoted Chubais as saying.
